purpose: Protected scoring baseline, not current presentation

choices.label: How much the snack breaks in a consistent handling test
choices.why: A repeatable observation connects directly to the project problem.

choices.label: Which wrapper colour looks most exciting
choices.why: The wrapper colour does not measure snack breakage.

choices.label: How to promise the longest shelf life
choices.why: Shelf life is a different question and has not been studied.

beats.whenWrong: Mass, physical firmness and people’s responses are different measurements.

beats.whenRight: You kept recorded events separate from ideas to investigate.
beats.whenWrong: What you saw or measured is evidence. A proposed cause still needs a test.

choices.label: Use A and B as planned, keeping all other conditions the same
choices.why: This tests the planned ingredient balance while holding the method steady.

choices.label: Change the binder, mixing time and shape together
choices.why: Several changes make it harder to tell which one affected the result.

choices.label: Make only B and compare it with a memory of A
choices.why: A remembered result is a weak comparison with no consistent control.

beats.whenRight: The plan defines the samples; the records connect the measurement to the recommendation.
beats.whenWrong: You need a defined plan and identified samples before a result can support a conclusion.

rows.label: A has ingredient amounts and its test method recorded.
rows.why: Those records support identifying and repeating the trial.

rows.label: B’s draft record omits the test method.
rows.why: The team must restore the verified method record so the result can be interpreted.

rows.label: C has no confirmed ingredient identity.
rows.why: Unknown ingredients must be checked before this sample can be used.

rows.label: D is held separately while its record is checked.
rows.why: Holding an uncertain sample protects against using it by mistake.

beats.whenRight: You identified missing evidence without treating a sensible hold as a defect.
beats.whenWrong: The problems are B’s missing method and C’s missing ingredient identity.

choices.label: Keep C out of tasting and ask Yuki to confirm the checks
choices.why: Unknown ingredient and allergen status must be resolved before tasting is considered.

choices.label: Taste a tiny piece to see whether it seems safe
choices.why: A small taste cannot establish allergen status or safety.

choices.label: Offer C without mentioning the missing record
choices.why: The colleague would be deciding without essential information.

beats.whenRight: You reduced expectation and group-pressure clues while keeping the comparison consistent.
beats.whenWrong: Use neutral codes, consistent conditions and independent responses.

beats.whenRight: You connected the real question, the measured result and a proportionate next test.
beats.whenWrong: Keep the recommendation within the handling evidence: less breakage in this trial, then a repeat comparison.

choices.label: Record that shelf life is unknown and ask the quality team to plan the required study
choices.why: The handling evidence does not answer the shelf-life question. A qualified team must define the appropriate work.

choices.label: Promise months of safe storage because B broke less
choices.why: Mechanical breakage is not evidence of safe storage life.

choices.label: Use the panel’s texture response as a safety certificate
choices.why: People’s texture responses do not establish product safety.
